doc.title: Joe Bushkin interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 15, 1999

title: Career pressure, learning from failure, Armstrong-Goodman tour
summary: Natural talent brings pressure; he learns from failures, and recalls the Armstrong-Goodman tour with Louis.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Yes, and he very much — Communications and Development. He’s a very important figure in the history of the college actually.
Yeah well I’m sure he had a full professorship going at least.
Did you ever have any inkling that you were NOT going to make a career in music? That you might do something else? Was there any question in your mind from the time you were a —

No, I was really kind of stuck with it. There’s a little pressure that goes on when you have a natural talent you know. Because you’ve got to live up to it and really produce and be creative when you’re called upon. And there are many days, they talk about the right place at the right time, that doesn’t happen as often as playing the gig you know? And as a matter of fact, you learn — I don’t know how to put this — but you learn from your failures and you don’t learn from your successes. You know?

And once you listen to a tape of an old 78 or a vinyl, you say now I could have done this better or that better, as a matter of fact I think it’s interesting from a jazz point of view when I did the Louis Armstrong/Benny Goodman tour and I played with Louis, as Louis put it, we were walking in the rain one afternoon and he kind of looked over at me and he said “you’re with the right Benny. You’ve got the right Benny on.” Meaning in that kind of language, a Benny is a raincoat. And because the fact that I was with Benny’s band after the war for a year, ten months or whatever it was, and I wrote a bunch of things for him, which we recorded, as a matter of fact Ernie — well I was delighted to be with Louis. It was a happy quintet. It was really fun.
